5       B. WIC’s Proposed Claims                                         
6       The Court’s stated commitment to attempt to expeditiously attempt to resolve this 
7  case on the merits also means it will address WIC’s Motion now. WIC seeks leave to 
8  intervene and file a complaint in intervention asserting three claims through the APA: two 
9  NEPA claims and one claim under the NHPA. (ECF No. 179-1 at 39-44.) One NEPA claim 
10  is for failure to take the requisite hard look at the impacts of the Project on cultural and 
11  archeological resources in the project area, in part because Defendants did not adequately 
12  consult with WIC. (Id. at 39-40.) The second NEPA claim is for failure to engage in 
13  government-to-government consultation with WIC before approving the ROD. (Id. at 40-
14  41.) And WIC’s proposed third claim is for violation of the NHPA because Defendants 
15  issued the ROD without first adequately determining which Indian tribes to consult, and 
16  without meaningfully consulting with WIC. (Id. 41-44.) Thus, all three of WIC’s proposed 
17  claims share a key allegation in common: Defendants did not meaningfully consult with 
18  WIC before issuing the ROD. (See generally id.)                       
19       WIC’s allegations are notable because Defendants have contended thus far in this 
20  case that they consulted with WIC, but WIC never raised any objections about the 
21  Project—and that evidence has gone unrebutted. (ECF No. 92 at 17.) WIC’s allegations 
22  are also notable because the Court has previously rejected for lack of prudential standing 
23  RSIC’s efforts to assert that Defendants did not meaningfully consult with the other tribes 
24  Defendants say they consulted with, including WIC. (ECF Nos. 92 at 7, 117 at 4-8.) WIC’s 
25  proposed claims accordingly set up a factual dispute that was not previously properly 
26  raised in this case about the quality of consultation between Defendants and WIC. At least 
27  at this stage, WIC appears to primarily allege that Defendants should have done more 
1  than simply send them letters for BLM’s consultation with WIC to have been compliant 
2  with NEPA or NHPA. (See generally ECF No. 179-1.)

15 ||  Ill.    WIC’S MOTION TO INTERVENE 
16          The  Court first  turns  to  WIC’s  Motion  before  addressing  other  parties’  motions 
17 || regarding the case schedule.  WIC seeks  intervention as of right under Fed.  R.  Civ.  P. 
18 || 24(a), or in the alternative, permissive intervention under Fed. R. Civ. P. 24(b). (ECF No. 
19 || 179 at 2.) The Court finds that WIC has not met either standard despite the liberal standard 
20 || generally  favoring  intervention.  The  Court's  analysis  below  focuses  on_  practical 
21 || considerations. 
22          A.  Legal Standard 
23          Rule  24(a)(2)  permits  anyone  to  intervene  as  of  right  who  “claims  an  interest 
24 ||  relating to the property or transaction that is the subject of the action, and is so situated 
25 ||  that disposing of the action may as a practical matter impair or impede the movant’s ability 
26 ||  to protect its interest,  unless existing  parties adequately represent that interest.” When 
27 || evaluating motions to intervene as a matter of right, courts construe  Rule 24 liberally in 
28 ||  favor of potential intervenors, focusing on  practical considerations rather than technical 

1  distinctions. See Sw. Ctr. for Biological Diversity v. Berg, 268 F.3d 810, 818 (9th Cir. 2001). 
2  A party seeking to intervene as of right must meet four requirements: 

3       (1) the applicant must timely move to intervene; (2) the applicant must have 
        a significantly protectable interest relating to the property or transaction that 
4       is the subject of the action; (3) the applicant must be situated such that the 
        disposition of the action may impair or impede the party’s ability to protect 
5       that  interest;  and  (4)  the  applicant’s  interest  must  not  be  adequately 
        represented by existing parties.                                 
6                                                                        
7  Arakaki v. Cayetano, 324 F.3d 1078, 1083 (9th Cir. 2003) (citation omitted). An applicant 
8  for intervention bears the burden of showing that all four requirements are met. See United 
9  States v. Alisal Water Corp., 370 F.3d 915, 919 (9th Cir. 2004) (citation omitted). 
10       Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 24(b)(1)(B) permits a court to allow anyone to 
11  intervene who submits a timely motion and “has a claim or defense that shares with the 
12  main action a common question of law or fact.” “An applicant who seeks permissive 
13  intervention must prove that it meets three threshold requirements: (1) it shares a common 
14  question of law or fact with the main action; (2) its motion is timely; and (3) the court has 
15  an independent basis for jurisdiction over the applicant’s claims.” Donnelly v. Glickman, 
16  159 F.3d 405, 412 (9th Cir. 1998) (citation omitted). But a court may still deny permissive 
17  intervention even if proposed intervenor satisfies those threshold factors. See id. And 
18  because a court has discretion in deciding whether to permit intervention, it should also 
19  consider whether intervention will cause undue delay or prejudice to the original parties, 
20  whether the applicant’s interests are adequately represented by the existing parties, and 
21  whether judicial economy favors intervention. See Venegas v. Skaggs, 867 F.2d 527, 530-
22  31 (9th Cir. 1989).                                                   
23       B. Discussion                                                    
24       The Court first addresses the timeliness of the Motion because that is a factor the 
25  Court  must  consider  before  it  grants  either  intervention  as  of  right  or  permissive 
26  intervention and then addresses the other factors.                    
27  ///                                                                   
1       1.   Timeliness                                                  
2       “Timeliness is ‘the threshold requirement’ for intervention as of right.” League of 
3  United Latin Am. Citizens v. Wilson, 131 F.3d 1297, 1302 (9th Cir.1997) (quoting United 
4  States v. Oregon, 913 F.2d 576, 588 (9th Cir. 1990)). “Timeliness is determined by the 
5  totality of the circumstances facing would-be intervenors, with a focus on three primary 
6  factors: ‘(1) the stage of the proceeding at which an applicant seeks to intervene; (2) the 
7  prejudice to other parties; and (3) the reason for and length of the delay.”’ Smith v. Los 
8  Angeles Unified Sch. Dist., 830 F.3d 843, 854 (9th Cir. 2016) (citation omitted). The Court 
9  addresses below WIC and Lithium Nevada’s arguments as to each of the three timeliness 
10  factors. The Court does not address timeliness twice (another time under a permissive 
11  intervention  heading)  because  an  ‘“alternative  request  for  permissive  intervention  is 
12  necessarily untimely’ when movant fails to satisfy the timeliness element for intervention 
13  as of right.”’ Chevron Env’t Mgmt. Co. v. Env’t Prot. Corp., 335 F.R.D. 316, 329 (E.D. Cal. 
14  2020) (citing Stadnicki on Behalf of LendingClub Corp. v. Laplanche, 804 Fed. App’x 519, 
15  522 (9th Cir. 2020)). And as further explained below, WIC’s Motion is untimely. 
16                 a.   Stage of the Proceeding

21  several substantive orders, and the parties are now on the eve of merits briefing. (ECF 
22  No. 185 at 3-4.) The Court agrees with Lithium Nevada.

26  lithium—with knock on national security and clean energy transition effects—and would 
27  sanction WIC’s approach of sitting silently through the environmental review process and

13       And though only Lithium Nevada explicitly argues as such, further delay in this case 
14  will  prejudice  all  parties.  Because  the  Court  has  declined  to  issue  any  preliminary

18  obtain on the merits of their claims would be less meaningful if Lithium Nevada has already 
19  irrevocably disturbed in the ground in the Project area—to the extent Lithium Nevada has 
20  not already done so under prior authorizations. And the Court agrees with Lithium Nevada 
21  that the financial harm it highlights as the prejudice it will suffer from the likely delay were 
22  WIC permitted to intervene is a cognizable harm under these circumstances. See, e.g., 
23  Battle Mountain Band v. United States Bureau of Land Mgmt., Case No. 3:16-cv-0268-
24  LRH-WGC, 2016 WL 4497756, at *10 (D. Nev. Aug. 26, 2016). Thus, the Court finds that 
25  the likely delay caused by WIC’s intervention would prejudice the other parties to this case.   
26                 c.   Reason for and Length of the Delay                
27       WIC argues that was it compelled to intervene by the Court’s November 2021 order 
1  order denying their motion for a preliminary injunction, where the Court reaffirmed its 
2  finding that those tribes lacked prudential standing to assert claims on behalf of WIC and 
3  the other tribes who were consulted in the environmental review process leading up to the 
4  ROD. (ECF No. 179 at 6.) Thus, WIC seems to argue it believed that either RSIC or the 
5  Burns Paiute Tribe were representing its interests up until the Court issued that order, and 
6  its delay of about three months from that date until WIC filed its Motion is reasonable. (Id.) 
7  Lithium Nevada counters that WIC has been aware of the Project for a long time and does 
8  not proffer a compelling reason for its delay in filing its Motion. (ECF No. 185 at 5-9.) As 
9  further explained below, the Court agrees with Lithium Nevada.        
10       A “party seeking to intervene must act as soon as he knows or has reason to know 
11  that his interests might be adversely affected by the outcome of the litigation.” California 
12  Dep’t of Toxic Substances Control v. Com. Realty Projects, Inc., 309 F.3d 1113, 1120 (9th 
13  Cir. 2002) (citation and emphasis omitted). WIC did not do so here. Indeed, WIC’s 
14  argument that the Court’s November 2021 order denying reconsideration prompted it to 
15  intervene is unpersuasive for several reasons.                        
16       First, the Court’s November 2021 order denying reconsideration merely reiterated 
17  the Court’s finding from its September 2021 order that RSIC and the Burns Paiute Tribe 
18  lacked prudential standing to assert claims on behalf of WIC and similarly situated tribes. 
19  (ECF Nos. 92, 117.) And WIC does not explain in its Motion why it picked the November 
20  order as its trigger date instead of the September order. (ECF No. 179 at 6.) In its reply in 
21  support of the Motion, WIC primarily restates the unchallenged general rule that the crucial 
22  date for assessing timeliness of a motion to intervene is when proposed intervenors should 
23  have been aware that existing parties would not protect their interests. (ECF No. 194 at 6-
24  7.) This mere restatement does not really explain why the November order is the crucial 
25  one instead of the September order. And to the extent that WIC is taking the view that the 
26  Court’s September order did not become final until the Court issued the November order 
27  denying reconsideration, that view is unpersuasive because it is possible that no party 
1  might not be represented by existing parties when the September order issued than when 
2  the  November  order  issued.  And  the  focus  of  the  timeliness  inquiry  is  on  notice 
3  (constructive or actual) not when an order becomes final in the sense of whether an 
4  existing  party  could  file  a  motion  for  reconsideration.  See  California  Dep’t  of  Toxic 
5  Substances Control, 309 F.3d at 1120.                                 
6       Second, the Court’s prudential standing rationale as to tribes like WIC rested on a 
7  longstanding “general prohibition on a litigant’s raising another person’s legal rights[.]” 
8  (ECF No. 117 at 5 (citation omitted).) The longstanding nature of this general prohibition 
9  means that neither the November order nor the September order was a reasonable trigger 
10  point where WIC should have become aware that existing parties to the case may not 
11  adequately represent its interests. WIC should have known all along that RISC, the 
12  People, and the Burns Paiute Tribe could not adequately protect its interests because it is 
13  not similarly situated to those tribes (or subset of a tribe, in the People’s case) as to the 
14  ROD. The difference is that BLM sent at least one letter requesting that WIC consult on
